title_en: Xingli Company and Guang'ao Company v. India International Trade Company, Malaysia Balapur Company, Kupak Company, and Nalin Company — appeal over cargo ownership dispute
keywords_en: Civil; Dispute over Ownership of Goods; Second Instance; Supreme People's Court; Beijing Municipality; Guangdong Province; Legal Person; State Organ; General Principles of the Civil Law; Civil Procedure Law; Attribution of Ownership of Goods; Bona Fide Acquisition; Validity of Bill of Lading; Upholding Original Judgment; Carriage of Goods by Sea; Forged Bill of Lading; Sale of Goods; Good Faith; Dispute over Ownership of Goods of Nalin Company
full_text_en:
Xingli Company and Guang'ao Company v. India National Trading Co., Ltd., Balapur Palm Oil Co., Ltd. (Malaysia), Kupak Co., Ltd. (Malaysia), Nalin Industrial Co., Ltd. (Malaysia) — Appeal Dispute over Ownership of Goods

Appellant (Defendant at First Instance): Liquidation Group of Beijing Xingli Service General Corporation Guangdong Company.

Appellant (Defendant at First Instance): Guangdong Shantou Special Economic Zone Guang'ao Commercial Service Development Company.

Appellee (Plaintiff at First Instance): India National Trading Co., Ltd.

Appellee (Plaintiff at First Instance): Balapur Palm Oil Co., Ltd. (Malaysia).

Appellee (Plaintiff at First Instance): Kupak Co., Ltd. (Malaysia).

Appellee (Plaintiff at First Instance): Nalin Industrial Co., Ltd. (Malaysia).

Appellee (Third Party at First Instance): Hong Kong Ligao Hong.

The appellants, Liquidation Group of Beijing Xingli Service General Corporation Guangdong Company (Xingli Company) and Guangdong Shantou Special Economic Zone Guang'ao Commercial Service Development Company (Guang'ao Company), dissatisfied with the civil judgment of first instance rendered by the Guangdong High People's Court, filed appeals respectively with the Supreme People's Court of the People's Republic of China in the case concerning a dispute over ownership of goods with the appellees, India National Trading Co., Ltd. (India National Trading), Balapur Palm Oil Co., Ltd. (Malaysia) (Balapur Company), Kupak Co., Ltd. (Malaysia) (Kupak Company), and Nalin Industrial Co., Ltd. (Malaysia) (Nalin Company). The Supreme People's Court, upon trial, finds as follows:

On May 21 and 22, 1985, India National Trading entered into four contracts with Balapur Company, Kupak Company, and Nalin Company (Malaysia) for the purchase of palm fatty acid distillate, on CIF Mumbai terms, at a unit price of USD 435 per ton, with the seller to arrange insurance. On June 26, 1985, India National Trading entered into a contract with Malaysia Rubber Development Co., Ltd. for the purchase of grade 3 smoked sheet rubber and Standard Malaysian Rubber 20, on C&F Madras terms, at USD 802 per ton for grade 3 smoked sheet rubber and USD 725 per ton for Standard Malaysian Rubber 20, with the buyer to arrange insurance. Pursuant to the contracts, Balapur Company, Kupak Company, Nalin Company, and India National Trading respectively arranged insurance with insurance companies. From July 2 to 15, 1985, Balapur Company, Kupak Company, and Nalin Company loaded 7,873 drums (totaling 1,456.485 tons) of palm fatty acid distillate, and Malaysia Rubber Development Co., Ltd. loaded 500 tons of grade 3 smoked sheet rubber and 2,000 tons of Standard Malaysian Rubber 20 purchased by India National Trading, onto the cargo vessel "Tropical Queen" owned by Panama Express Shipping Company. On July 23, 1985, the "Tropical Queen" departed from Port Klang, Malaysia, bound for Madras, India. After August 5, contact with the ship's agent was lost. Following the disappearance of the "Tropical Queen", Balapur Company, Kupak Company, and Nalin Company received full compensation from the insurance companies and issued "subrogation certificates" to the insurers. India National Trading received only partial compensation from its insurer.

On August 25, 1985, through the introduction of Zhou Qianwen, manager of Hong Kong Xiangquan Company, the appellant Xingli Company and Guang'ao Company entered into a sales confirmation (Guangshang Jin Zi No. 047) with Hong Kong Ligao Hong (Ligao Hong) for the purchase of 300 tons of grade 3 rubber (at USD 745 per ton) and 1,460 tons of grade 20 rubber (at USD 700 per ton). Guang'ao Company also entered into a sales confirmation (Guangshang Jin Zi No. 048) with Ligao Hong for the purchase of 1,456 tons of industrial palm oil (at USD 155 per ton). The two sales confirmations stipulated: the shipping mark of the goods was "Tavalos Hope", and insurance was to be against FPA (Free of Particular Average). Payment was to be made in full within four months after the goods arrived and passed inspection; if the goods did not meet national standards, the parties would negotiate a price based on quality.

On August 29, 1985, Liao Minqiang, manager of Ligao Hong, informed Guang'ao Company that the vessel "Tavalos Hope" carrying the goods had arrived in the waters outside Shantou Port, China, and asked Guang'ao Company to handle customs clearance procedures. He handed Guang'ao Company an undated invoice and two "original bills of lading" for the cargo, but without accompanying insurance documents. The two bills of lading recorded: 7,873 drums of palm oil, 1,760 tons of natural rubber, port of loading Kaohsiung, port of discharge Shantou, cargo mark number N/M (i.e., no mark). Guang'ao Company took delivery of the goods discharged from the "Tavalos Hope" based on these bills of lading. The rubber, lacking an import license, was placed under customs supervision and storage. From August 30 to September 27, 1985, at the request of Ligao Hong, Guang'ao Company commissioned the Shantou Ocean Shipping Agency to refuel the "Tavalos Hope" and pay crew wages, etc., totaling USD 167,800. This amount was advanced by Guang'ao Company, with the agreement that it would be deducted from the payment due to Ligao Hong. From October 1985 to April 1986, because the palm fatty acid distillate risked deterioration, Guang'ao Company sold all of it except for five drums retained as samples.

In September 1985, the insurance companies that had insured India National Trading, Balapur Company, Kupak Company, and Nalin Company learned that a vessel named "Tavalos Hope" was anchored at Shantou Port, China, discharging a batch of palm fatty acid distillate and rubber. Upon investigation, the insurers believed that the "Tavalos Hope" was the former "Tropical Queen", and that the goods discharged from this vessel were the goods lost by the four Indian and Malaysian companies. After multiple unsuccessful attempts to recover the goods through negotiations with Guang'ao Company, the four Indian and Malaysian companies filed a lawsuit against Guang'ao Company as defendant with the Guangdong High People's Court on June 28, 1986. The Guangdong High People's Court, upon accepting the case, added Xingli Company as a defendant and Hong Kong Ligao Hong as a third party.

After trial, the Guangdong High People's Court found: Guang'ao Company discharged 7,873 drums of palm fatty acid distillate from the "Tavalos Hope". The markings on the drums—including the name, gross weight, net weight, country of origin, supplier name, production date, packaging date, port of loading, port of discharge, and consignee name—were consistent with the markings recorded in the original straight bills of lading, purchase contracts, and quality certificates held by Balapur Company, Kupak Company, and Nalin Company. However, they were inconsistent with the "original bills of lading" for the cargo provided by Ligao Hong to Guang'ao Company, which described the goods as palm oil, port of loading Kaohsiung, and port of discharge Shantou. Guang'ao Company discharged 318.3939 tons of grade 3 smoked sheet rubber and 1,248.7127 tons of Standard Malaysian Rubber 20 from the "Tavalos Hope", and the outer packaging marks matched those recorded in the original straight bills of lading and quality certificates held by India National Trading. The court further found that after the disappearance of the "Tropical Queen", it was renamed "Tavalos Hope", retaining Panamanian registry; that the "Tavalos Hope" did not call at Kaohsiung Port at any time in 1985, so there was no loading at Kaohsiung; and that the original bills of lading for the cargo provided by the third party to the two defendants, which stated that the goods were loaded at Kaohsiung Port, Taiwan, on August 7, 1985, were inconsistent with the facts.

The Guangdong High People's Court held: This case involves a dispute over ownership of goods. The "Tavalos Hope" was the former "Tropical Queen" after renaming, and the goods discharged at Shantou Port were the goods lost by the four plaintiffs. The four plaintiffs respectively hold non-negotiable original straight bills of lading for the disputed goods and are the owners of the goods, entitled to assert ownership rights against the possessors and sellers. The requests of the four plaintiffs for the two defendants to return the goods and to refund the amount of goods sold by the defendants based on net invoice value should be granted. The third party, Ligao Hong, by providing forged bills of lading, sold goods it had no right to sell, violating the international trade practice that a seller must ensure that no third party can assert any right or claim over the goods sold. Its conduct was void, and it has no right to claim the goods or payment from the defendants in this case. It shall bear primary responsibility for the expenses incurred from the import of the goods due to its void conduct. The two defendants, by violating the "Interim Regulations on the Licensing System for Import Goods of the People's Republic of China" (Provisional Regulations on Import Licensing), illegally imported rubber. The defendant Xingli Company, by violating the "Regulations on the Administration of Registration of Industrial and Commercial Enterprises" (Regulations on Registration Administration), engaged in import trading beyond its registered business scope, and its conduct was void. The two defendants cannot rely on their void conduct to acquire ownership of the disputed goods, and they shall bear corresponding responsibility for the expenses incurred in the import of the goods. During the period when the "Tavalos Hope" was anchored at Shantou Port, Guang'ao Company, at the request of Ligao Hong, advanced USD 167,800 for refueling, crew wages, and living expenses for the vessel. This conduct violated the international practice that only the shipowner or its agent is authorized to commission a shipping agent to handle port entry procedures and internal ship affairs. This amount shall be recovered by the defendants from Ligao Hong on their own. Based on the above, the Guangdong High People's Court ruled:

1. The subject matter of this dispute belongs respectively to the plaintiffs.

2. The sale transactions between the two defendants and the third party concerning the subject matter of this dispute are void. The two defendants shall return to the plaintiff India National Trading the 318.3939 tons of grade 3 smoked sheet rubber and 1,248.7127 tons of Standard Malaysian Rubber 20, which are under customs supervision and storage, in their current condition. Expenses incurred during the return period shall be borne by the plaintiff itself.

3. The two defendants shall return to the plaintiffs Balapur Company, Kupak Company, and Nalin Company the 7,868 drums of palm fatty acid distillate already sold (1,455.58 tons) at the net invoice value of USD 615,476.86 as claimed by the plaintiffs, and shall return the five retained drums of samples to the three plaintiffs in their current condition.

4. The expenses incurred in the import and storage of the disputed goods, totaling RMB 844,977.91, shall be borne by Ligao Hong in the amount of RMB 506,986.75, and jointly by the two defendants in the amount of RMB 337,991.16.

The defendants Xingli Company and Guang'ao Company, dissatisfied with the judgment of first instance, filed appeals with the Supreme People's Court. Their appeal grounds: There is no direct legal relationship between the appellants and the four Indian and Malaysian appellee companies, and the appellees have no right to pursue the goods or claim compensation against the appellants as defendants. After the loss of their goods, the four appellees each received compensation from their respective insurance companies; according to insurance practice, they can no longer bring an action in their own name as the original owners. The sales activities between the appellants and Ligao Hong constitute normal international private trade; under the principle of the seller's implied warranty of title, the appellants have full ownership of the disputed goods. The appellants did not violate the "Provisional Regulations on the Licensing System for Import Goods" nor exceed their business scope. The sales contracts between the appellants and Ligao Hong are valid and lawful. They request the appellate court to remand the case to the court of first instance for retrial or to amend the judgment, and to order the four appellees to compensate the appellants for economic losses arising from this case.

The appellees India National Trading, Balapur Company, Kupak Company, and Nalin Company responded: The determination of the litigation positions of the parties and the order for the appellants to return goods and payment to the appellees in the judgment of first instance are correct and should be affirmed. They request the appellate court to dismiss the appellants' appeal and order the appellants to compensate the appellees for interest losses on the long-term storage of the disputed goods due to the appellants' unreasonable appeal.

During the second instance, both the appellant Guang'ao Company and the appellee India National Trading agreed to dispose of the rubber promptly to prevent further deterioration. Both parties provided to the court letters of guarantee from creditworthy banks for USD 1,222,428. By order of the Supreme People's Court, the disputed rubber was handed over to Guang'ao Company for disposal, with the proceeds deposited in the Shantou Branch of the Bank of China.

The Supreme People's Court held: The court of first instance correctly identified the essence and main content of this dispute as a dispute over ownership of goods. A bill of lading is a document of title; the holder of the bill of lading is the owner of the goods under the bill. When the goods under a bill of lading are possessed by another, the holder of the bill of lading is entitled to bring an action against the possessor for confirmation of ownership and return of the goods.

After the loss of the goods, the four appellees each claimed compensation from their respective insurance companies. Among them, the three Malaysian companies received full compensation from their insurers and issued "subrogation certificates" to the insurers. According to the international practice that the law of the insurer's location governs insurance contracts, the insurance matters concerning the three Malaysian companies are governed by Malaysian law. Under Malaysian law, the ownership of the goods remains with the insured. India National Trading received only partial compensation from its insurer and is also entitled to bring an action in its own name. Therefore, the four appellees are lawful plaintiffs in the first instance, and the two appellants, who possess the disputed goods, are lawful defendants in the first instance. The appellants' contention that the four appellees have no right to pursue the goods or claim compensation from them is unfounded.

The court of first instance, based on the marks and packaging indicators on the original straight bills of lading, purchase contracts, and quality inspection certificates provided by the four appellees, and after verifying that the marks and packaging indicators on the outer packaging of the disputed goods matched those documents, correctly determined that the four appellees, who hold the original straight bills of lading, are the owners of the disputed goods. Consequently, it correctly found the sales transactions between the two appellants and Ligao Hong void, that Ligao Hong has no right to claim from the two appellants goods that do not belong to it, and that Ligao Hong shall bear primary liability for losses caused by its void conduct.

The appellant Guang'ao Company, by violating the "Provisional Regulations on the Licensing System for Import Goods", illegally imported rubber. The appellant Xingli Company, by violating the "Regulations on Registration Administration" issued by the State Council of the People's Republic of China, engaged in import rubber trading without foreign trade business qualification. The court of first instance correctly held that the illegal conduct of the two appellants was one of the causes of the invalidity of the sales confirmation (Guangshang Jin Zi No. 047) regarding rubber.

During the second instance, the appellant Xingli Company further raised: After Guang'ao Company and Ligao Hong signed the sales confirmation (Guangshang Jin Zi No. 048) concerning the purchase of industrial palm oil, the appellant merely signed and sealed on the sales confirmation held by the buyer Guang'ao Company. The court of first instance's finding that Xingli Company also participated in signing the No. 048 sales confirmation is inconsistent with the facts and should be overturned. Upon investigation, this contention of Xingli Company is true. The cause of the invalidity of the Guangshang Jin Zi No. 048 sales confirmation is that Ligao Hong sold goods it had no right to sell. The appellant Guang'ao Company, when accepting the goods, knew that the transaction was for industrial palm oil but took delivery of palm fatty acid distillate; the sales confirmation specified the mark as "Tavalos Hope", but the bills of lading delivered by Ligao Hong had no mark, while the actual goods taken had marks inconsistent with both documents. Guang'ao Company was negligent in accepting the goods. Due to the invalidity of the No. 048 sales confirmation and its own negligence, Guang'ao Company cannot acquire ownership of the palm fatty acid distillate. The appellants' contention that their sales transactions with Ligao Hong are valid and lawful and that they have acquired ownership of the disputed goods through those transactions is unfounded.

The palm fatty acid distillate in dispute has been sold by the appellant Guang'ao Company in its entirety except for five drums retained as samples. The appellees Balapur Company, Kupak Company, and Nalin Company's request for compensation from the appellant Guang'ao Company for interest losses on the value of that cargo during the appeal period should be granted.

Accordingly, the Supreme People's Court, pursuant to Article 151(2) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, on September 1, 1990, renders the following judgment:

1. Affirm item 1 of the original judgment;

2. The transactions for rubber between the appellants Guang'ao Company and Xingli Company and the appellee Ligao Hong are void. Guang'ao Company shall refund to the appellee India National Trading the amount guaranteed by the Shantou Branch of the Bank of China for the prior disposal of the rubber, totaling USD 1,222,428;

3. The transactions for palm fatty acid distillate between the appellant Guang'ao Company and the appellee Ligao Hong are void. Guang'ao Company shall refund to Balapur Company, Kupak Company, and Nalin Company the net invoice value of the palm fatty acid distillate as recorded in the transactions between those companies and India National Trading, totaling USD 615,476.86. The five drums of retained samples shall be returned to the said three companies in their current condition. Expenses incurred during the return period shall be borne by the said three companies themselves;

4. The appellant Guang'ao Company shall compensate Balapur Company, Kupak Company, and Nalin Company for interest losses on the value of the palm fatty acid distillate from June 1, 1988, to August 31, 1990, totaling USD 96,937.61;

5. The expenses incurred in the import and storage of the disputed goods, totaling RMB 920,267.71, shall be borne by the appellee Ligao Hong in the amount of 60%, i.e., RMB 552,160.63, and jointly by the appellants Guang'ao Company and Xingli Company in the amount of 40%, i.e., RMB 368,107.08.
